content: Liver spots, also referred to as age spots, sun spots, lentigos, or senile/solar lentigines, are skin blemishes that develop as a result of aging and prolonged exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun. These spots vary in color, ranging from light brown to black, and are commonly found on areas of the skin that are frequently exposed to sunlight, such as the hands, face, shoulders, arms, and forehead. Despite their name, liver spots are not associated with the liver. The term liver spots originates from the resemblance of their coloration to that of the liver. Starting around the age of 40, the skin's ability to regenerate from sun damage diminishes, making liver spots a frequent occurrence in older individuals, particularly those who spend significant time outdoors in the sun. In some cases, emotional distress has been observed to contribute to the proliferation of these spots. In the vast majority of cases, liver spots are benign and do not require medical treatment. However, in rare instances, they may obscure the detection of skin cancer, which necessitates careful evaluation. Some individuals find liver spots cosmetically undesirable and may choose to have them removed for aesthetic reasons. Removal options include cryotherapy or laser treatment. For diagnosis, a physical examination of the skin is typically performed. Visual assessment of the spots, often guided by dermatological references such as a dermatology atlas, aids in confirming the diagnosis of liver spots.
